hints: Notice this question tests two separate Group 17 ideas, displacement by a more reactive halogen and oxidation by concentrated sulfuric acid.
Remember reactivity decreases down Group 17, so chlorine displaces bromine and iodine, but bromine cannot displace chlorine and iodine cannot displace bromine.
Think about reducing strength of halide ions, chloride is too weak to be oxidised to chlorine by the acid, but bromide is strong enough to be oxidised to bromine.
walkthrough:
**Recall the halogen displacement rule**

A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide from solution. Reactivity order is key here.

$$\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2 \text{ in oxidising power}$$

**Recall the reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid**

Chloride ions are weak reducing agents, so they only do acid-base reaction to give hydrogen chloride gas. Bromide ions are stronger reducing agents, so they reduce the acid and are themselves oxidised to bromine.

$$\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HCl}$$

$$2\text{HBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Apply both ideas to the statements**

Bromine cannot free chlorine from $\text{NaCl}$ because bromine is less reactive than chlorine. Iodine cannot free bromine from $\text{NaBr}$ because iodine is less reactive than bromine. Only bromide with concentrated sulfuric acid correctly gives free bromine.

options.A: Incorrect. Concentrated sulfuric acid with sodium chloride gives only white fumes of hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$, not chlorine. Chloride ion is not a strong enough reducing agent to reduce sulfur from +6 in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
options.B: Incorrect. Bromine is below chlorine in Group 17 and is less reactive, so it cannot oxidise chloride ions to chlorine. Only a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one, so chlorine would displace bromine, not the reverse.
options.C: Correct. Bromide ions are stronger reducing agents than chloride ions. Concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises $\text{HBr}$ (formed first) to orange bromine vapour, $\text{Br}_2$, while itself being reduced to $\text{SO}_2$.
options.D: Incorrect. Iodine is below bromine in Group 17 and is less reactive, so it cannot oxidise bromide ions to bromine. Bromine would displace iodine from iodide, not the reverse.
